rules.statement: Register an opt-in capability that layers on another library's services as an extension on that library's marker-typed service builder (`IServiceBuilder<TMarker>`), not on a bare `IServiceCollection`.
rules.why: The receiver marker proves at compile time that the prerequisite library is registered; a bare collection gives the compiler nothing to enforce, so a missing prerequisite becomes a confusing runtime failure.
rules.check: Look for new `Add…` extension methods on `IServiceCollection` that hook, decorate or consume another library's services instead of extending that library's `IServiceBuilder<TMarker>`.

rules.statement: Express a registration's second prerequisite as a required `IServiceBuilder<TMarker>` parameter (the builder that prerequisite's registration returned), never as a marker struct value or a bespoke proof type, and return the receiver builder.
rules.why: Anyone can `default` an empty marker struct, so a marker instance proves nothing; only a builder minted by the prerequisite's registration is unforgeable, and returning the receiver keeps the chain on the primary library.
rules.check: Look at registration methods with an extra prerequisite: is it a parameter of marker type, an optional or nullable builder, or a custom proof type, and does the method return something other than its receiver?

rules.statement: Encode registration prerequisites only in the builder types; don't add runtime checks that verify another library was registered.
rules.why: Runtime verification defers an avoidable mistake to startup and depends on order, while the typed builders make a missing prerequisite or a wrong order a compile error.
rules.check: Look for registration code that inspects the service collection (for example `IsRegistered`, `Any(d => d.ServiceType == …)`) or throws to signal a missing prerequisite library.

rules.statement: Every registration that another registration depends on, including a dependency-inverted seam such as a custom store, must mint and return its own marker-typed builder.
rules.why: Dependents can only demand an unforgeable witness if the prerequisite's registration hands one back.
rules.check: Look at store and seam registrations that dependents need: do they return `void` or the bare collection instead of `IServiceBuilder<TheirMarker>`?

rules.statement: Define a registration marker as an empty `readonly struct` implementing `IRegistrationMarker<TMarker>`, and put a library's marker in that library's `.Abstractions` package.
rules.why: The marker's type identity is the whole signal, so it carries no data to keep in sync. Abstractions-only consumers must be able to name the builder without referencing the implementation package.
rules.check: Look for new marker types that are classes, have members or data, or are declared in an implementation package rather than in the `.Abstractions` package.

rules.statement: Take a bare `IServiceCollection` only for registrations that stand alone: chain roots that bootstrap a marker with no prerequisite, one-service helpers, and marker-less cross-cutting infrastructure.
rules.why: The test is whether the registration would do the right thing if it were the only thing registered; anything that hooks another library's services is a bolt-on and must gate on that library's builder.
rules.check: For each new bare-collection extension, ask whether it depends on services from another library; if so, flag it.

rules.statement: A helper that is called from more than one library's builder should extend the non-generic `IServiceBuilder`, not a bare `IServiceCollection` and not one specific marker builder.
rules.why: The non-generic builder still requires the caller to hold some library builder, so it is stronger than a bare collection, and it doesn't tie the helper to one library.
rules.check: Look for shared helpers (message factories, endpoint providers or groups) that extend `IServiceCollection` or a single `IServiceBuilder<TMarker>` even though several libraries use them.

rules.statement: Follow the registration naming shape: a package-root `AddXLibrary()` extends its prerequisite's builder, creates its own builder with `NewBuilder<XLibrary>()` and returns it; a folder-level `AddYServices()` extends `IServiceBuilder<XLibrary>` and returns its receiver; a bolt-on returns the builder it augments.
rules.why: A bolt-on adds to an existing library and introduces no new library layer, so only library roots mint new builders.
rules.check: Look at return types: does a bolt-on or a folder-level registration mint a new library builder, or does an `AddXLibrary` return its receiver instead of the new builder?

rules.statement: Name a package's main registration class `DefaultRegistration`, and put each other receiver shape or opt-in set in a sibling `…Registration` class, because one static class holds only one `extension(...)` receiver.
rules.why: Analyzer CA1708 forbids mixing receivers in one static class, and the naming keeps registration code easy to find.
rules.check: Look for a static class with `extension(...)` blocks for more than one receiver, or registration classes named outside the `DefaultRegistration`/`…Registration` pattern.

rules.statement: In host wiring, compose capabilities by chaining off the builders the single composition root exposes, never by calling capability methods on the bare `IServiceCollection`, and reference implementation packages only from the composition root.
rules.why: Chaining off the root's builders documents the dependency order at the call site and keeps the compile-time prerequisite checks in force.
rules.check: Look in host or sample startup code for capability registrations called on `services` directly, or for implementation-package references outside the composition root.
